headline: HALF A SENTENCE FROM MOSCOW, A JOLT FROM BRASÍLIA, AND THE FED ON DECK

bullets.html: Dec Chicago settled Monday at $6.15½, down 9½¢, after trading as high as $6.27½. The $6.12½ low broke Wednesday's $6.21 and the July 9 low at $6.18, the first two lines on Saturday's map. KC settled at $6.58½, down 5½¢, and Minneapolis at $6.34, down 7½¢. Overnight, Dec is quiet near $6.14, holding above Monday's low.

The trigger came from Moscow. Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Alexander Alimov told Interfax that Russia is examining proposals for safe grain shipping across the Black Sea and is talking with Turkey. In the same breath he said he sees no prospect of reviving the grain deal, per the Moscow Times. The market sold the first half of the sentence.

Brazil re-elected President Lula 51.8% to 48.2% on Sunday, an outcome its markets hadn't positioned for. The real fell about 12% against the dollar and São Paulo stocks tripped a circuit breaker, per Al Jazeera. November soybeans fell 15¼¢, and wheat went with them.

The Fed meets today and announces Wednesday at 11 a.m. Pacific. It raised rates in September for the first time since 2023, per Fox Business. A hold is expected this week, but futures put the odds of a December hike near 80%, per CNBC. The dollar index is 102.04 this morning, up 4.07% this year.

Box-o-Rox: EXECUTE. Monday was the 14th straight settle below the Suspend/Execute line, which sits near $6.96, about 80¢ above the market. The Tripwire is down to about $6.67¼. No discretionary hold is in effect. Box-o-Rox informs; the marketing plan decides. See the chart and the rules →

PNW soft white held its $6.25 bid for October and November Monday while Chicago lost 9½¢. In one session, the bid went from even with Dec futures to 9½¢ over them, per Northwest Grain Growers. The ladder still runs 5¢ a month to $6.45 in March.

Russia starts buying its own wheat. The government plans to put up to 3 MMT into its intervention fund to support farmers who can't move grain past damaged ports, per UkrAgroConsult. Interfax puts the start at Thursday, per Total Farm Marketing.

U.S. wheat inspections were 6.8 million bushels last week. The season total is 273 million, 35% behind last year, against a USDA forecast of 750 million, per TFM. Winter wheat is 76% planted and 53% emerged, each one point behind average, per USDA via DTN.

Ahead: Wednesday, the Fed at 11 a.m. Pacific. Thursday, export sales, and Russia's buying begins. Friday, COT. Clocks fall back Sunday. Midterm elections are next Tuesday, Nov. 3. The WASDE lands Nov. 10 at 9 a.m. Pacific, and the three-way talks can start any time after that.

body.html: Saturday we wrote that a pause isn't a turn, but most turns start with one. We also wrote that the quiet ends when one side commits. Monday, the sellers committed. Dec Chicago bounced overnight to $6.27½, above Friday's close. Then one headline out of Moscow took the market down through Wednesday's $6.21 low and the July 9 low at $6.18, to $6.12½. It settled at $6.15½, down 9½¢. Bloomberg puts the most-active contract at its lowest since July 9, and says the market has now effectively lost the Black Sea risk premium it carried since summer. That was the first session of what could be a ninth straight losing week. So this morning's question isn't whether the slide is over. It's what exactly the market sold on Monday, and whether it was worth selling.

The market heard half a sentence. Here's the whole sentence. Alexander Alimov, Russia's deputy foreign minister, told Interfax that Russia is examining proposals from several countries for safe grain shipping across the Black Sea and is in contact with Turkey. Then he said, "But for now, I don't see any prospects for reviving the 'grain deal,'" per the Moscow Times. Wheat traded the first half and ignored the second. Dmitry Rylko of IKAR, the Moscow consultancy, explained the pattern: since the season began, "any positive signals suggesting a potential improvement in shipping conditions have pushed futures prices lower," per UkrAgroConsult. Andrey Sizov of SovEcon called last week's optimism "premature," per Investing.com. Paris milling wheat lost €7.25 Monday, to its lowest since mid-August, per TFM. Wednesday the market heard a promise to talk. Monday it heard a promise to think about it. Neither one moved a single ship.

Even peace doesn't reopen the lanes overnight. Shipments through the Azov and Black Sea ports have been largely halted since mid-August, per Investing.com. Russia is now routing wheat out through the Baltic. IKAR quotes 12.5% protein wheat at $264 a tonne FOB from Vysotsk and Ust-Luga, down $3 on the week, and SovEcon has it at $270, down $5. Those ports sit more than 1,000 miles north of Novorossiysk as the crow flies, and a great deal farther by sea. Bloomberg's sources add a point the market has skipped past: even if security improves, a quick return to the old routes is unlikely, because many importers have already moved to other suppliers and costlier logistics, per UkrAgroConsult. The market is pricing a peace that, even if it comes, would refill the pipeline slowly. That's an uneven trade. A deal that arrives takes weeks to show up on a vessel lineup. A deal that falls apart shows up on the screen that morning.

Then Moscow told its own farmers something else. On Oct. 20, Deputy Prime Minister Dmitry Patrushev said the state would buy up to 3 MMT of grain, class 3 and 4 wheat plus rye, into its intervention fund. The stated purpose is to support producers who can't sell grain because of logistics problems and port damage, per UkrAgroConsult. Agriculture Minister Oksana Lut said early this month that the buying would begin at the end of October, per NeMoskva, and Interfax puts the start at Thursday, Oct. 29, per TFM. The Russian consultancy ProZerno estimates this season's export shortfall at 14 to 20 MMT, so 3 MMT covers only about 15 to 20% of the grain that can't get out, per UkrAgroConsult. It's a gesture, not a floor. Read the behavior, not the headline. A government that expects its export lanes to reopen soon doesn't spend money to take grain off its own farmers' hands. It does that when it expects them to stay stuck. That's Moscow's own read on the shipping talks, and it costs more than a quote to Interfax.

The biggest wheat headline of the weekend came out of Brasília. Brazil's runoff went to the incumbent, 51.8% to 48.2%, and markets had positioned for the challenger. The real fell about 12% against the dollar Monday, and stock trading in São Paulo stopped for 30 minutes on a circuit breaker, per Al Jazeera. The quickest hit landed on soybeans. A cheaper real makes Brazilian beans cheaper to the world, and Nov soybeans fell 15¼¢ to $12.41¼, per Brownfield. TFM tied wheat's drop partly to that soybean slide. The wheat angle runs deeper, and the headlines haven't reached it yet. Brazil is on track for record wheat imports this season. Estimates run from about 7 to more than 8 MMT, with the domestic crop down, per DataMar. Back in May, the head of Abitrigo, Brazil's millers' association, said mills expected to import 1 to 1.5 MMT from origins outside South America's Mercosur trade bloc, with more coming from the U.S. and Russia, per DataMar. That's the long-haul wheat, paid for in dollars, and as of Monday it costs a Brazilian mill about 12% more in reais than it did Friday. The arithmetic says Brazil's millers lean harder on Argentina's big crop and buy less from farther away. That's an inference, not a report yet. It's still worth watching in Thursday's export sales.

Crude is bearish wheat by the back door. Saturday we said the scissors were still open, with energy pricing a wider war while wheat prices a peace. Here's the hinge between the blades. War-driven energy costs pushed the Fed to raise rates on Sept. 16, its first hike since 2023, to a range of 3.75% to 4%, per Fox Business. The 2-year Treasury yield now sits at 4.72%, pricing more hikes to come. The dollar index is 102.04 this morning, up 0.39 since Friday and 4.07% higher this year, and less than a point under its Oct. 14 high of 102.735. Every point on that index makes a bushel of U.S. wheat a little harder to sell overseas. So the oil that isn't lifting wheat is lifting the dollar against it. WTI is $102.05 this morning, down $1.22 since Friday, and still above $100. A hold is the near-unanimous call for Wednesday. What matters is what Chair Kevin Warsh says about December, when futures price roughly an 80% chance of another hike, per CNBC. The decision comes at 11 a.m. Pacific Wednesday, a week before the midterms.

Our class held its bid. On Monday, Chicago lost 9½¢ and the soft white bid didn't move. It stayed at $6.25 for October and November delivery, $6.30 December, $6.35 January, $6.40 February and $6.45 March, for Portland delivery, per Northwest Grain Growers. Friday that $6.25 bid sat even with Dec Chicago. By Monday's close it was 9½¢ over. A 9½¢ stronger basis in one session, on a down day, says the buyers behind soft white still want the wheat, and it fits Saturday's export numbers, with soft white sales only 4½% behind last year while HRW runs 63% behind. Kansas City offered its own clue. Saturday we wrote that KC's slide was long liquidation and that long liquidation runs out of longs to sell. Monday KC lost 5½¢ to Chicago's 9½¢, and its premium over Chicago widened from 39¢ to 43¢. One session doesn't make a trend. It's the first sign the KC selling may be tiring.

Scout the terrain, revised. Monday spent the first two lines on the map, so here's the new one, on the Dec contract. Overhead, $6.18 and $6.21 were floors last week and are the first ceilings now. Above them, the Aug. 11 floor at $6.45¼, then the Tripwire near $6.67¼. Below, the weekly retracement mark at $6.06¼, the July 1 low at $6.02½, and the June 30 summer low at $5.90½. On the 30-minute chart, the overnight has held between $6.13 and $6.17 and never tested Monday's low. A falling line from Thursday's high crosses near $6.16 to $6.17 this morning. That's the first thing a bounce has to clear. It's a map, not a forecast.

Box-o-Rox: EXECUTE. Monday was the 14th straight settle below the Suspend/Execute line. That line sits near $6.96, about 80¢ above the market. The Tripwire fell another 3¾¢ to about $6.67¼. No discretionary hold is in effect. A return to SUSPEND would take a settle back above the Suspend/Execute line, and that's a long way up from here. The benchmark's record is on the chart: 83% of the 2026 crop priced as of Oct. 1. Those are Monday's settlement figures. This morning's chart includes the overnight session, so its lines read a little lower.
Marketing posture: EXECUTE, on plan. This week, let the cash market do the work.

• Producers: If the plan calls for a sale this week, the elevator's bid hasn't moved against you. The board has. Soft white is $6.25 this morning, the same as Friday, with Chicago 9½¢ lower. Every soft white grower in the region is looking at that same bid, and it's the best-looking number on the screen. The resting offers you set over the weekend still stand. Add $6.18 to $6.21 as the first rung, since that's the first place a bounce runs into last week's sellers.

• Unpriced wheat in the bin: Saturday's carry math still holds. The ladder pays 20¢ from November to March, a little under 10% a year on $6.25 wheat. Now set it against the note. The prime rate has been 7% since banks followed the Fed's September hike, and most operating lines price above prime. If December brings another quarter point, the gap between what the ladder pays and what the bank charges gets thinner. Run that number Wednesday afternoon, after the Fed, not before.

• Millers, feeders and end users: Monday's 9½¢ came off half a sentence, against a market where Black Sea logistics won't snap back even if the talks succeed. Funds are heavily short in Chicago. The downside left in a peace headline is shrinking. The upside in a stalled talk isn't. Breaks like Monday's are where coverage gets extended, in scale.

• Merchandisers: Watch three things this week: the KC–Chicago spread for a second session of KC strength, Thursday's export sales for the first sign of whether Brazil's currency shock reaches U.S. wheat, and the dollar index's Oct. 14 high at 102.735 after Warsh speaks.

• Lenders and elevator managers: Mark unpriced inventory at $6.15½, then run it at $6.02½ and $5.90½. Then run the borrower's operating line at a quarter point higher. Both are live possibilities before Christmas.

Here's the part that doesn't fit in a bullet. Wheat is $1.79½ off its Sept. 2 high, down 23%. Diesel, on the NY Harbor contract, is $4.77 a gallon, about 51¢ off its Sept. 15 all-time high, down less than 10%. That gap is the squeeze in plain numbers. What the crop brings fell more than twice as far as what it costs to grow the next one, with the operating note and the fertilizer bill still to come. Retail anhydrous averaged $987 a ton in the second week of October, 18% above a year ago, and urea $674, up 13%, per DTN. Weeks like this one try to turn a marketing plan into a referendum on the whole operation. Don't let them. A diplomat in Moscow who said "maybe" and "no" in the same breath doesn't get to set what your wheat is worth. Neither does a vote in Brasília. The number you wrote down Saturday does. If the market comes to it, take it. If it doesn't, the plan was built for exactly this kind of week, so that no one at the kitchen table has to make the call cold at 7:30 in the morning.

This stuff is trackable. Let's track it.
Stay tuned.
—Gabe
